section_title: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
summary: This assessment unit details the status and trends of global carbon stocks in soil and biomass, the impact of land degradation on net primary production, and the environmental consequences of atmospheric and soil pollution, including nitrogen deposition and pesticide use.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3 Changes in carbon stocks following degradation and restoration
passages.text: In warm, dry years, associated especially with El Nino climate events, the global land sink weakens sharply, to the point where the land may become a small net source of carbon to the atmosphere.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.1 Loss and recovery of soil carbon
passages.text: Soil organic matter changes under degradation and restoration in both quantity and form, because of changes in the balance between carbon inputs (plant litter, manure) and outputs (product exports, mineralization, and erosion).

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.1 Loss and recovery of soil carbon
passages.text: Soil inorganic carbon – common in arid lands as calcrete – is less responsive than soil organic carbon to human-induced change.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.1 Loss and recovery of soil carbon
passages.text: Owing to the centrality of SOC to fertility, low values and negative trends have been proposed as an index of degradation.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.1 Loss and recovery of soil carbon
passages.text: The soil organic carbon loss in cultivated soils results from reduced carbon inputs of plant litter (since the net primary production may be reduced relative to the original vegetation, and a large fraction is harvested for human or animal use) and increased carbon outputs through heterotrophic respiration, stimulated by the action of ploughing.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.1 Loss and recovery of soil carbon
passages.text: Soils typically lose carbon under human use but can also recover (sequester) the lost carbon and productivity upon implementation of management practices that favour carbon inputs over outputs and reduce soil erosion.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.2 Loss of terrestrial biomass and carbon sequestration
passages.text: Anthropogenic land degradation generally reduces net primary production, which is why it changes in net primary production can be an indicator of land degradation.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.2 Loss of terrestrial biomass and carbon sequestration
passages.text: Recent analyses suggest a net sink in arid and semi-arid ecosystems, attributed to the effect of rising atmospheric CO2 on plant water use efficiency (and hence net primary production).

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.2 Loss of terrestrial biomass and carbon sequestration
passages.text: The fraction of net primary production remaining after the human appropriation is what is available to non-domesticated organisms; thus, rising human appropriation of net primary production is at the expense of biodiversity.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.3.3 Degradation of peatlands
passages.text: Natural peatlands are, on balance, generally greenhouse neutral or have a slight cooling effect on the global climate, whereas damaged peatlands are substantial emitters of CO2.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.4.1 Atmospheric pollution
passages.text: Increased near-surface ozone concentrations, largely as a consequence of nitrogen oxides, methane and non-methane volatile compounds in the presence of sunlight and exacerbated under climate change, decrease crop yields.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.4.1 Atmospheric pollution
passages.text: Elevated atmospheric nitrogen deposition contributes to the eutrophication of soils causing changes in plant species composition and diversity in unmanaged terrestrial ecosystems; increases in emissions of nitrous and nitric oxides; and elevated runoff of nitrate resulting in eutrophication of fresh and coastal waters.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.4.2 Soil pollution
Agriculture
passages.text: The wide-scale use of synthetic and organic fertilizers has far reaching environmental impacts, including air pollution, soil acidification and degradation, accumulation of trace metals, crop yield reduction, and eutrophication of both inland and coastal waters.

heading_path: 4. STATUS AND TRENDS OF LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
4.2.4.2 Soil pollution
Agriculture
passages.text: Pesticides affect a range of soil processes, including decomposition of organic matter and infiltration of rainwater. Herbicides generally are less deleterious to soil organisms than insecticides and fungicides, but significantly reduce plant biodiversity.
